name: Anvil Row Forge

bio: Heavy-gauge steel work cut in a converted apple-orchard shed at the base of Mt Hood. Brothers Eli and Sam Reeves run the place — Eli on the plasma table, Sam on the powder gun. We obsess about edge finish and won't ship a piece until the welds disappear under the topcoat.
name: Cascade Iron Works
workshop_intro: In 2016, we cleared out a derelict apple-sorting shed on the south side of Hood River to make room for a load of scrap plate and a salvaged welder. Eight years later, that same shed houses our 5x10 CNC plasma table and a custom-built powder coating booth. We operate as a two-man shop at the base of Mt. Hood, where Eli handles the CAD programming and torch height control while Sam manages the finish work. We built this business on a refusal to accept the burred, jagged edges common in mass-produced steelwork. Every piece that leaves our bench undergoes a multi-stage hand-sanding process to ensure the perimeter is smooth before it hits the rack. We obsess over the transition between the metal and the finish, ensuring our welds are ground flush and completely hidden beneath the final coat. If the structural integrity or the edge profile is anything less than clean, the piece stays in the shop. This is how we handle steel.

bio: Custom metal signage and farmhouse name plates from a hill-country workshop outside Fredericksburg. Built around a 4x4 fiber laser and a stubborn respect for hand-rubbed finishes. We've made signs for ranches, breweries, and three of the best BBQ joints in the state — every piece leaves with a burn-marked maker's mark on the back.
name: Hill Country Forge
workshop_intro: We started Hill Country Forge in 2013 after salvaging an industrial press brake from a shuttered machine shop in San Antonio. What began as a project to replace the rusted-out entrance gates on our family land outside Fredericksburg turned into a decade of refining the intersection of heavy steel and high-precision optics. Today, our workflow centers on a 4x4 fiber laser and a dedicated hand-patina bench where we process every piece of plate steel. While the laser provides the accuracy required for complex ranch brands and brewery logos, we refuse to automate the final surfacing. We spend hours on the hand-rubbed finish of each sign, rejecting the thin, uniform appearance of powder coating in favor of a depth that only manual oxidation and oil can achieve. The Texas sun is hard on metal, so we build for the long term. Every name plate and sign is finished until the texture feels right under a thumb, then stamped with our maker's mark. We produce work that holds its ground.

bio: Hybrid maker — we pour epoxy rivers through black walnut slabs in the mornings and run our plasma table in the afternoons. The work that happens at the seam between wood and steel is what we live for. Studio tucked into a converted barn outside Asheville, runoff from the French Broad about a mile north.
name: Appalachian Steel & Slab
workshop_intro: We started in 2017 after pulling a saturated black walnut log out of a creek bed near the French Broad River and realizing the local mills wouldn't touch wood that erratic. That first slab sat in the back of the barn for a year while we figured out how to stabilize it. Today, the work is dictated by our 5x10 CNC router and a 4x8 plasma table that handles the heavy plate steel. Most of our mornings are spent around the pressure pot, ensuring the epoxy resin is forced into every void and checking for clarity that lesser pours miss. We refuse to use pre-mixed wood stains or chemical accelerators to mimic age. Every slab is finished with a hand-rubbed oil process that takes three days longer than a spray-on lacquer but ensures the wood can breathe in the humid North Carolina summers. The structural integrity of the seam where the metal meets the grain is the only metric that matters to us. This is how we build furniture meant to outlast the house it sits in.

bio: Industrial-strength functional fabrication out of Michigan's Upper Peninsula. We don't do decorative — we do brackets that hold three generations of shelving, machine guards that pass MIOSHA on the first walkthrough, and tool-wall systems built around your actual setup. Quote turnaround is 24 hours; we send a sketch with every bid.
name: Great Lakes Fabworks
workshop_intro: The foundation of Great Lakes Fabworks was laid in 2010 when we spent a winter in a sub-zero Marquette garage rebuilding a collapsed gantry crane for a local timber mill. That project solidified our preference for overbuilt structural integrity over aesthetic pretense. Today, our workflow centers on a 6kW fiber laser and an Amada press brake that allows us to hold tolerances within thousands of an inch on heavy-gauge plate. We refuse to compromise on the deburring process; every edge is hand-finished to ensure no slag or sharpness remains before the metal leaves the bench. In the Upper Peninsula, equipment has to survive harsh conditions and heavy use, so we source domestic cold-rolled steel that handles the thermal shifts of the region without warping. We provide a technical sketch with every quote to ensure the geometry meets your specific load requirements. We build things intended to outlast the buildings they inhabit.

bio: Fiber laser studio at the edge of the Sierra Nevada. We make our living on the things plasma can't touch — sub-millimeter detail engraving, personalized boards, coordinates plaques, intricate map work. Quiet shop, sharp output.
name: BlackRiver Laserworks
workshop_intro: We began this work in 2018 when a series of heavy winters in Truckee pushed us into a small, heated garage to experiment with high-frequency marking on cold-rolled steel. Our operation is built around two primary workhorses: a 100W CO2 laser for deep timber engraving and a dedicated fiber marking laser used for surgical-level detail on hardwoods and metals. While many shops prioritize speed to increase volume, we refuse to compromise on our multi-pass finishing process. This requires running the machines at a fraction of their rated speed to ensure every coordinate plaque and topographical map has the tactile depth that single-pass engraving lacks. The high-altitude air here is dry, which affects how wood fibers react under the beam, so we calibrate our settings daily to account for the material's moisture content. We do not use filler or paint to hide shallow burns. The clarity of the final mark is the only metric that matters in this shop.

bio: Small-batch artistic metal shop tucked into a converted feed barn in the upper Arkansas valley. We build layered steel wildlife scenes — aspen groves, wolf packs, alpine vistas — that catch the same light the actual landscape does outside our shop door.
name: Emberline Metalworks
workshop_intro: We started in 2015 when a heavy winter in the upper Arkansas valley collapsed a neighbor’s outbuilding, leaving us with a salvageable pile of plate steel and a curiosity about what we could pull from the wreckage. Since then, we have spent nine years refining a process that bridges high-precision engineering with the jagged geometry of the Rockies. Most days are spent between the 4x8 Plasma CNC table and our 3kW Fiber Laser, cutting silhouettes that mimic the shift of light across the Sangre de Cristo range. We refuse to compromise on the post-cut edge; every piece undergoes a multi-stage mechanical grinding process to remove dross and heat tint before it ever sees a TIG welder. This manual refinement ensures that while the computer provides the accuracy, the hand provides the finish. We work out of a converted feed barn in Salida where the mountain air dictates our drying times and the landscape informs every line we cut. We make objects that are meant to be felt as much as seen.

bio: Commercial fabrication shop building branded signage for storefronts, breweries, ranches, and outdoor outfitters across the northern Rockies. We deliver in person to clients within 300 miles — that's the radius we can drive and be back by dinner.
name: NorthForge Customs
workshop_intro: We started in 2012 after a heavy winter storm collapsed a neighbor's ranch gate near Bozeman, leaving us to piece it back together with a borrowed stick welder and a grinders worth of patience. Twelve years later, our process has shifted toward more sophisticated tolerances, but the mechanical grit remains the same. Most of our heavy plate work originates on the 6x12 fiber laser, while the custom bracketry and thicker structural components are cut on the heavy-duty plasma CNC. We refuse to compromise on the final deburring process, ensuring every edge is radiused by hand to remove the dross and heat-affected zones that automated shops often overlook. This level of physical finishing is what allows our signs to hold up against the wind shear and freeze-thaw cycles common across the northern Rockies. When a piece leaves the shop, it is either loaded onto our mobile install rig for a regional delivery or crated for long-haul freight. Our work is built to outlast the buildings they are bolted to.

bio: Three-person CNC carving studio focused on landscape-inspired wall reliefs. We work almost entirely in figured western maple and reclaimed redwood — slow species, careful tool paths, a stepover small enough that the carved surface feels milled to glass by hand.
name: Redwood CNC Collective
workshop_intro: In 2013, we recovered a single fallen figured maple log near the Eel River that was too wide for any local mill to process. We spent that winter rigging a makeshift carriage just to slab it, and we have spent the eleven years since perfecting the way we translate those complex grains into topographical forms. Today, our workflow centers on a heavy-frame 5x10 CNC router and a custom-built 4-axis indexer used for more complex rotational reliefs. While the machinery handles the bulk of the material removal, we refuse to compromise on tool path density. We run our finishing passes with a stepover so minute that the machine time triples, ensuring the redwood and maple surfaces emerge from the deck with a glass-like clarity that requires minimal sanding. Living and working among the fog-heavy forests of Eureka dictates a slower pace of drying and stabilization. We do not rush the wood, and we do not skip the thousandths of an inch that define a clean edge. The machine provides the geometry, but the grain dictates the finish.

bio: Modern architectural metal studio in the high desert. We build decorative wall pieces for interior designers, hospitality clients, and luxury residential builds — brushed brass, copper, anodized aluminum. Geometric, refined, photo-ready under any lighting.
name: CopperEdge Makers
workshop_intro: We started in 2016 when a local architect in Sedona asked us to solve a light-reflection issue on a massive copper facade that was blinding drivers at sunset. That project forced us to move beyond hand tools and invest in the precision required for large-scale architectural metalwork. Today, our workflow centers on a 6kW fiber laser for clean-edge geometry and a CNC press brake that allows us to hit exact angles in heavy-gauge brass and aluminum. Between these stages, every piece spends hours in our vibratory polishing tank to ensure the surface grain is uniform across the entire batch. We refuse to use pre-finished sheets from a supplier because the edges never match the face. Instead, we grain every surface in-house after the cuts are made, ensuring the metal holds its character under direct gallery lighting. The high desert dust stays outside the shop while we focus on the micron-level tolerances required for interior installations. We build these pieces to be the permanent technical standard of a room.

bio: Hybrid hardwood and steel workshop on the northern Idaho panhandle. We build functional furniture — floating shelves, console tables, wall cubbies — at the intersection of two materials. Joinery matters. Welds matter. The seam between the two matters most.
name: Forge & Grain Workshop
workshop_intro: In 2011, we began by salvaging structural steel from a decommissioned mill site outside Sandpoint, realization hitting that the raw industrial scrap required a more refined counterpart in local timber. Thirteen years later, our process centers on the deliberate union of these two elements. We rely on a 4x8 CNC router for precision joinery and a dedicated TIG station for the clean, stacked welds necessary when steel remains exposed. While the equipment has evolved, we maintain a stubborn refusal to use edge banding or veneer; every shelf and console table leaves the shop as a solid slab, finished by hand through our drum sander until the grain transition is seamless. The northern Idaho climate dictates how we season our hardwoods, ensuring the timber survives the shift from our humid workshop to a dry interior environment without checking. We focus our energy on the structural integrity of the seam where metal meets wood. The work is built to be heavy, permanent, and indifferent to trends.
